machatzit-hashekel/1:_: (s.k. 1) And if he passed, etc. — even in a dark house. Meaning: a fortiori where there is daylight one cannot use a candle by day, as stated "a candle in daylight — what use is it"; but even in a dark house one cannot, and he gives a reason from Yerushalmi that a candle does not shine by day as it shines at night.
machatzit-hashekel/2:_: (s.k. 2) And a portico, etc. — and it has no wall. Chayei Adam disagrees and wrote that even if it has three walls and is open on the fourth side it is called a portico — see there.
machatzit-hashekel/3:א: (s.k. 3) If he checked — and in the Gemara it states, etc. — since these words of Shas are needed in their places in this siman, for many laws flow from them, I will copy: Our Rabbis taught: one does not check by sunlight, nor by moonlight, nor by torchlight, but by candlelight, because candlelight is good for checking, etc. And we asked: this sunlight — how so? If we say in a courtyard — but Rava said the middle of a courtyard (so Rambam's text) need not be checked because ravens are found there; rather in a portico. And Rava said a portico is checked by its light. And it answers: it is not necessary except for a skylight in a room; and how so — if alongside the skylight, that is like a portico; rather from the sides — end of Shas daf 8. From this it implies a portico is checked even l'chatchila by its light: one, the language "is checked by its light" implies l'chatchila; and further, if so what does it ask from the baraita — the baraita teaches how one checks by sunlight, i.e. l'chatchila, and with this Rava agrees; it cannot be that Rava who said "is checked" means b'dieved. Bach wished to settle the questioner's difficulty: it would seem sunlight is like moonlight and torchlight that even b'dieved do not help — see there; but this is somewhat strained, since the baraita speaks only of l'chatchila law and not b'dieved — how is it relevant to say "like" regarding something the baraita does not discuss. Therefore Magen Avraham wrote to settle what implies in the Gemara that even l'chatchila is permitted: when he checked by day — meaning he forgot to check at night by candlelight and comes to check by day; although everywhere even when checking by day one needs candlelight, a portico he checks even l'chatchila without a candle but only by its light. What implies in Shulchan Aruch is Rambam's language specifically b'dieved, because l'chatchila he must check on the night of the 14th and not rely to check by day by its light. Now it is resolved what the Gemara asks on Rava from the baraita that states one does not check l'chatchila: it means l'chatchila one must check on the night of the 14th; now it is well said it is like moonlight — meaning even when the moon shines, i.e. at night, one does not check by it; and likewise sunlight when the sun shines, i.e. by day, and nevertheless it teaches one does not check l'chatchila. If so there is no dispute here, unlike Bach who wrote three disputes: Rashi's view that even l'chatchila they check on the 13th by its light — he wrote: "is checked by its light and need not bring candlelight at night, rather checks by day" — end; Bach wrote so is Rif's view; Ri'az and as appears Rosh's view: on the 13th one does not check, but on the 14th one may check l'chatchila by sunlight; Rambam's view, which is Shulchan Aruch's language, that even on the 14th l'chatchila he does not check except by candlelight — end. Per Magen Avraham's words there is no dispute, for certainly Rambam and Rosh are clear from Magen Avraham's words that they do not disagree, as explained; but nevertheless it appears Rashi disagrees, as explained. However, after investigation it comes out well that in this law Magen Avraham discusses there is no dispute and Rashi also agrees. For on the Sages' enactment that checking time is the night of the 14th and not the morning of the 14th, Rabbenu Nissim Beit Yosef daf 4 gave two reasons: when people are in their homes, and further because candlelight is good for checking (and although in the baraita above that one does not check by sunlight, etc., only one reason was mentioned — because candlelight is good for checking — one may say he cited one of them; also we do not find anyone who disagrees with Rabbenu Nissim Beit Yosef on this). If so, in a portico its light is great and equal to candlelight, and the reason "candlelight is good for checking" is not relevant there; nevertheless other reasons remain — "when people are in their homes, where will he go" — and so Kessef Mishneh explicitly in chapter 2 law 4: why one does not check a portico l'chatchila except at night — because people are present, etc. Therefore what Rashi wrote that they check it by its light l'chatchila on the 13th must mean he holds this reason "when people are in their homes" applies only to why we do not check on the morning of the 14th — because then most people have gone to work and perhaps one will forget and not come home until night, when Pesach has already entered and he transgresses "it shall not be seen"; unlike when he wishes to check on the 13th.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ב: He will come home only at night — then Pesach has already entered and he transgresses "it shall not be seen"; unlike when he wishes to check on the 13th — it appears forbidden, because then people are not in their homes and perhaps he will forget until night; and what of it if he forgets until night — then too people are not in their homes, but on the night of the 14th is the main time of checking. Rather on the 13th it is forbidden because candlelight is good for checking; and since a portico has great light, it is permitted to check it l'chatchila on the 13th and he need not wait until the night of the 14th. However there is another reason not to check on the 13th, as Mordechai brought in Magen Avraham s.k. 20: not to divide checking from checking.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ג: But it is possible Rashi disagrees with Mordechai on this; but for us who rule like Mordechai, one does not check a portico on the 13th, and in this we disagree with Rashi. From this law Magen Avraham did not speak here; but if he did not check the portico on the 13th and the night of the 14th arrived, in this all agree, also Rashi, that l'chatchila he must check at night and not wait until tomorrow on the 14th — meaning for Rashi too, even though one need not divide checking from checking, nevertheless it is forbidden to wait until the 14th because people are present, etc. If so Magen Avraham's words are resolved, and there is no dispute — meaning in this law Magen Avraham discusses: when standing on the night of the 14th l'chatchila, all require checking at night; b'dieved if he waited until day, all agree checking by its light suffices. Chayei Adam wrote: when he forgot to check at night and checks by day — whether a portico by its light or other places by candlelight — he should check in the morning because the diligent precede mitzvot, as stated daf 4a.
machatzit-hashekel/4:_: (s.k. 4) Opposite, etc. — therefore Ri'az wrote it is forbidden to check opposite the window, etc. Beit Yosef brought Ri'az's words: he wrote specifically a portico, but another house — even if it has great light — requires checking by candlelight. It appears he wrote so because of what they said regarding a skylight in a room, and he did not explain fully: it should mean specifically from the sides, but in the middle of the room one checks by the skylight's light — end Beit Yosef; and so Magen Avraham: Ri'az speaks where he wrote "but another house" like our houses that have no skylight but windows, and Ri'az holds even opposite the window is forbidden, for it is not like a skylight — with this what Ri'az left unspecified is resolved. It is likewise in Rambam — I did not know a clear meaning: Rambam did not copy the skylight law at all; if Bach meant to settle why Rambam omitted skylight because it is included in his words that a portico whose light is great, etc., and Rava said only a portico is checked by its light to explain so, to learn from it for every place whose light is great — end; therefore Magen Avraham holds a window is also included in "great light." Although a skylight's light is greater, nevertheless Rambam did not mention skylight at all — Magen Avraham should have inferred so. Also from other poskim: author of Tzitz Eliezer and Bach also for Rambam — he did not copy skylight intending as Bach said for Rambam; also other poskim did not copy skylight law except Tur — see Bach. Perhaps because Rambam wrote in chapter 5 law 4: one does not check, etc., nor by sunlight, etc. — in what case? in holes and hiding places; but a portico whose light, etc. — he only excluded holes and hiding places, implying opposite a window is permitted. Shulchan Gavoah wrote: they check by daylight, etc. — implying even, etc.; in Shas and poskim sunlight was mentioned and one would think specifically when the sun shines; but from Shulchan Gavoah who wrote "by daylight" it implies "by sunlight" is not precise.
machatzit-hashekel/5:א: (s.k. 5) And not by candle — for he separated them, etc. — for holes and cracks and lest he burn, etc. — so it should read: these are two reasons in the Gemara. Rabbenu Nissim Beit Yosef said because one cannot put it into holes and cracks; Rabeinu Peretz said because one fears lest he burn the house; there is a practical difference between these two reasons: for Rabbenu Nissim Beit Yosef, if he checks holes and cracks with a single candle, he may check the rest of the house with a torch; but for Rabeinu Peretz who gave the reason that one fears lest he burn the house, even in such a case it is forbidden. If so, even b'dieved, etc. But a tallow candle, etc. — I have seen people err and think all this follows to the end: why he separated into two clauses regarding torch mentioned in the Gemara which has many reasons, therefore even b'dieved he has not fulfilled. Unlike a tallow candle which is only a stringency, therefore b'dieved he has fulfilled; therefore he did not include them in one clause since their laws differ regarding b'dieved. Accordingly they ask: why did he include oil with tallow — he should have included oil with torch since he wrote oil has the law of a torch; but in truth this is not Magen Avraham's intent in his answer: what he wrote is because torch appears in the Gemara to forbid — and with this he concluded his answer. Meaning: since the others are only from custom stringency, and torch is forbidden by Gemara law, therefore he did not include them as one; but where their law is not the same regarding b'dieved, that does not cause separating into two clauses; and even if their law were the same, that would not cause including them in one clause. Afterward he wrote from his own reasoning:
machatzit-hashekel/5:ב: And there are many reasons, etc. — therefore since there are many reasons in it, one may say even b'dieved he has not fulfilled; unlike tallow, since there is no other reason except stringency lest it drip, etc., therefore it appears to Magen Avraham that in any case b'dieved he has fulfilled. Oil — since in any case there is another reason stated in the Gemara for torch that permits putting it into holes — therefore it appears to Magen Avraham that even b'dieved he has not fulfilled, like a torch. He wrote in Chayei Adam: if he has no wax candle he may take those candles with which in any case he fulfills, for a time of pressure is like b'dieved; he also wrote wood is forbidden because wood alone does not burn, and a torch is forbidden; even greased wood called kiyin that burns alone one should not take, because its smell is bad and sparks fly from it onto vessels, and we fear thereby he will not check well.
machatzit-hashekel/6:_: (s.k. 6) Even braided — this language is not in Maharil. Meaning: the Rama gloss derives from Maharil's words as written in Darkei Moshe, and in Maharil he did not write the language "even."
machatzit-hashekel/8:_: (s.k. 8) Less than, etc. — and if children, etc. — likewise the high places where a person's hand does not reach — if it is their practice to use there by ladder and the like, checking is also required.
machatzit-hashekel/9:א: (s.k. 9) Chicken coop — he wrote "and all in it," and it appears his intent, etc. — I am dealing with this: meaning two difficulties: first he brought Magen Avraham in the name of several poskim that chickens cause exemption from checking — how can he say "all in it" the opposite view that chickens cause obligation to check; rather it should say "they ate it."
machatzit-hashekel/9:ב: And further: if checking is required, what does sweeping help, as Magen Avraham wrote in this siman seif 11 that sweeping alone does not help, and nevertheless checking is required. Therefore sweeping suffices — meaning: although in this siman he wrote sweeping does not help, that is because of concern for leavening in holes that is not removed by sweeping; unlike a large piece that cannot be in a hole without coming out entirely outside the hole, and since in any case it comes outside it is well removed by sweeping — see s.k. 7 afterward where he agreed to the law in this.
machatzit-hashekel/9:ג: s.k. 7 here — and it is like clear chametz. Mahari Weil — so it should read.
machatzit-hashekel/10:א: (s.k. 10) But, etc. — and even if chametz remains there he does not transgress, for he declared it ownerless before its prohibition time; nevertheless if he finds chametz there after its prohibition time he must destroy it, as below siman 445. Because the essence of destroying chametz is burning or casting to the wind; when it lies in a courtyard dogs and animals will eat it. It is explained below siman 448 seif 6 in the name of Yerushalmi that after its prohibition time it is forbidden to give even to other animals or as ownerless; here although he does not give to them but they eat on their own, nevertheless l'chatchila it is good to destroy them, for doubt does not remove certainty — meaning: doubt "they ate it" does not remove certainty of chametz we know is there; as written at the beginning of siman 438: one saw a mouse enter with a loaf in its mouth and another enter after it and found crumbs even the size of the whole loaf — we do not say these crumbs are from this loaf; and since he found them again, no checking is required, for a mouse is not accustomed to crumble; therefore these crumbs are not from this loaf but from elsewhere, and the mouse entered with the loaf into the house — therefore checking is required. He infers from the unspecified wording that even a small loaf — and why not? when the loaf is large one could say "I ate it" — nevertheless for a small loaf one could say "I ate it"; or because the chametz is definite and "I ate it" is doubt, and doubt does not remove certainty. So too in the Gemara daf 9 on what we taught there: we are not concerned lest a weasel dragged from place to place — as Rashba wrote siman 434; and the Gemara inferred the reason: we do not see it take, but if we see it take, checking is required even if it says "I ate it" — because doubt "I ate it" does not remove certainty of chametz.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ב: And it is difficult: if so what does it ask, etc. — daf 8 as above in s.k. 3: since Rava speaks specifically of possible chametz, perhaps the baraita that teaches one does not check by sunlight refers to a courtyard — his courtyard with definite chametz, and Rava agrees checking is required; on this the baraita said one does not check by sunlight; and although in the baraita it teaches one does not check with definite chametz, the language of checking is not appropriate but language of destroying — as Ran brought, Beit Yosef siman 436. Nevertheless in truth it is not now definite chametz, for perhaps they ate it, but we do not rely on this since we know definite chametz was there; if so the language of checking fits well; and although it is still difficult why one does not check by sunlight, for it is not worse than a portico — as regarding skylight, if alongside the skylight, etc. — this is another question; but the Gemara's question that asks "but Rava said middle of courtyard need not checking" remains.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ג: Therefore even definite chametz need not checking, as stated in the Gemara, etc. — meaning: although doubt does not remove certainty, here there is certainly that they dragged it — this is the latter answer in the Gemara daf 9b; and although in the first answer there they do not say "certainly they dragged it," Rambam chapter 9 of Hilchot Tefillin ruled like the first answer — perhaps the Gemara and Semak do not hold like Rambam, and poskim hold like the latter answer that they say "certainly they dragged it." Further, Rambam did not rule like the first answer except because of doubt we go stringently, as Kessef Mishneh wrote there in chapter 9 of Hilchot Tefillin; but here regarding bedikat chametz which is d'rabbanan — d'oraisa nullification suffices — perhaps Rambam also agrees we go leniently and say "certainly they dragged it," for according to one answer Tosafot daf 9a in Pesachim s.v. so that it be, etc.: if he nullified, which is d'rabbanan, we say doubt comes and removes certainty of d'rabbanan.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ד: If so, in the mouse case it is well — meaning in siman 438 and Gemara daf 9 we well say doubt "it ate it" does not remove certainty, although certainly it dragged it — what of it? it nevertheless remained in his house, for mice drag into their holes.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ה: But ravens, etc. — meaning here in a courtyard we rely on ravens; and perhaps what Semak wrote is Shulchan Aruch's words "but definite chametz, no" — its source is not Semak; it appears to Magen Avraham strained to explain Semak speaks of birds found in a courtyard, for it is not a poskim's way to be cryptic — therefore he explained Semak really speaks in every case. What he wrote "but definite chametz, no" — meaning we do not say "they ate it"; here we speak where we say ravens ate it, and nevertheless we say they dragged it; on this he said nevertheless there is a difference if birds are found in the courtyard — we do not say "they dragged it." Chayei Adam asked: if so Magen Avraham's question returns on Bach in its place — what does it ask on Rava, perhaps the baraita speaks of definite chametz and birds found in the courtyard. In my humble opinion it is resolved: one — per what Chayei Adam himself wrote to settle what Magen Avraham wrote on Rambam who reads middle of courtyard need not checking — implying the sides require checking; if so what does it ask on Rava — it should have said the baraita speaks of the sides of the courtyard. Chayei Adam answered per Ran on Rambam's view: Ran — a courtyard need not checking; middle of courtyard — but holes require checking; so too Rambam — end; and since Rambam only exempts courtyard holes, the question no longer applies — it should have said the baraita speaks of courtyard holes, because there is no sunlight and the language "one does not check by sunlight" is not relevant — end Chayei Adam; with this Magen Avraham's words are also resolved — now the Gemara need not establish the baraita as definite chametz and birds found in the courtyard, for then the language "one does not check by sunlight" is irrelevant — necessarily if they ate it, what will he check, and if they did not eat it, certainly they dragged to their holes, as Rashi wrote daf 9b, and there is no sunlight, as explained. Also per Bach's words to settle Rambam who said middle of courtyard, etc. — Magen Avraham's words can be explained there. However, per Chayei Adam's understanding of Magen Avraham's words it remains difficult: "still it should be difficult — perhaps it speaks of definite chametz in a place where ravens are not found, only birds" — implying Magen Avraham agrees where both birds and ravens are found, no checking is required; therefore the baraita must be established where ravens are not found, only birds, and the law with him that where birds and ravens are found no checking is required because it is a double doubt: perhaps they ate it, and if you say they did not eat, nevertheless they dragged it — and whence that the birds in the courtyard dragged it, perhaps ravens dragged elsewhere. Accordingly it is difficult: the baraita should not speak where there are no ravens, only birds — for then how do we hang this question on Magen Avraham's words, for in any case it is difficult, for Rava gives the reason that a courtyard need not checking because ravens are found there — therefore the baraita should be established where ravens are not found; but one may say: do you take ravens from elsewhere? Even where ravens are not found, other birds wander after their food and one may rely on them; Rava mentioned ravens because in the amoraim's locale ravens were found, as they say regarding meat hidden from sight that perhaps ravens exchanged it — and there too ravens are not precise. If so, if we establish the baraita where there are no ravens or other birds coming from elsewhere, we find this only in a covered courtyard where a bird from elsewhere cannot enter; with this the language "one does not check by sunlight" is irrelevant, since when covered there is no sun, and even by daylight one cannot check. Also from what Bach wrote regarding a place where they regularly eat, etc. — this difference applies also to Magen Avraham's words, for Magen Avraham did not disagree with him except regarding ravens that we say "certainly dragged elsewhere," unlike here where it speaks of a house where ravens are not relevant but only birds in the house that drag to their holes, and one can only rely that they ate, and it is doubt that does not remove certainty. So too seif 8, etc. — "this is in general," etc. — behold although definite chametz requires a hoe and shovel, nevertheless in general nullification suffices; therefore although we know chametz was used there, nevertheless it is not called definite chametz, as Magen Avraham wrote, for there is much doubt.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ו: And what Bach wrote in the name of Rambam is not precise, etc. — meaning Bach came to support his answer that with definite chametz there is a difference: in his own courtyard forbidden, in partners' courtyard permitted, as explained, and brought proof from Rambam: Bach — it appears to me that for this Rambam was precise and wrote regarding a cattle shed and coops and the like that definite chametz requires checking, and did not write so regarding a courtyard — because the matter is not clear regarding a courtyard, since when not designated to one person, no checking is required — end; Magen Avraham wrote this refers to storehouses: Rambam chapter 2 law 16 — holes of the house, etc., roof, cattle shed, coops, hayloft, wine and oil storehouses from which one does not take mid-meal, large fish houses — no checking unless chametz was brought in — end; this "unless" when he adjoined storehouses, etc., means there no checking is not because we rely birds ate it, but because one does not take mid-meal — therefore we say he did not bring chametz there; on this he said specifically from the general case, but if he knows he brought chametz there, although one does not take mid-meal, checking is required; but regarding a shed, etc., where animals ate it, Rambam did not speak at all whether there is a difference between possible and definite chametz.
machatzit-hashekel/10:ז: And perhaps all thirty days, etc. — accordingly what he wrote in s.k. 6 before this, and where they eat all year and there are no chickens there — one must check under benches — implying if there are chickens, no checking and sweeping suffices, as he wrote before in the name of Beit Yosef, Darkei Moshe, Ri'az, Rashba, and Kol Bo; therefore it must mean within thirty days they did not eat there, or he was careful chametz did not fall under benches — otherwise even if there are chickens, checking is required, as he wrote here that doubt "they ate it" does not remove certainty. And I am dealing with siman 465: how should one conduct if he feeds his animal barley on Pesach.
machatzit-hashekel/11:_: (s.k. 11) And the rest, etc. — lest it rolled, etc. — so it should not be difficult why nullification is required, since a person's hand does not reach there — if so certainly he did not use chametz there. And so he wrote nevertheless nullification is required lest it rolled, etc.; Chayei Adam wrote in the name of Bach: but definite chametz must be removed, for it is like hiding in a pit. Chayei Adam wrote on him: chametz in a pit depends on the dispute between Rambam and Raavad siman 438, and we rule there like Rambam that nullification suffices, and so here; and in s.k. 17 Magen Avraham brought the Rambam-Raavad dispute there — what he wrote:
